Multi-omics has moved from a methodological aspiration to a routine design choice in molecular biology, and the conceptual rationale is no longer in dispute: simultaneous profiling of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and microbial layers captures interactions that no single assay can resolve [R1, R54]. What has lagged behind this conceptual maturation, however, is the software infrastructure that researchers must actually use. A typical multi-omics project now involves five to seven data types, several thousand samples and a downstream pipeline that spans preprocessing, integration, dimensionality reduction, clustering, biomarker discovery and visualisation. Each of those steps admits a dozen or more competing implementations, and the tooling has accumulated faster than the standards that should govern it. The result is an analytical gap that is no longer conceptual but infrastructural: researchers spend more time reconciling file formats, harmonising object classes and reproducing someone else's R environment than they do interpreting biological signal.

The heterogeneity of the available tools is striking. On the R side, Bioconductor provides the foundational data structures, most notably MultiAssayExperiment, which offers coordinated representation, storage and operation on diverse genomics datasets and ships with ready-to-analyse TCGA objects [R28]; on top of this substrate the community has built package-specific integrators such as mixOmics with its DIABLO supervised framework [R27], the longitudinal timeOmics [R20] and netOmics packages [R21], the vertical and horizontal miodin workflow [R48], the MOFA-based transfer-learning extension MOTL [R32], the MuSA radiogenomic GUI built on the same MultiAssayExperiment class [R25], and reproducibility-oriented wrappers such as moiraine that let users compare multiple integrators head-to-head [R3]. The Python ecosystem is no less crowded, ranging from graph-neural-network frameworks such as BioNeuralNet [R5] to specialised deep-learning integrators including MOADLN [R17], MCluster-VAEs [R22], MO-GCAN [R29], DeepMoIC [R12] and MoAGL-SA [R39]. Parallel to these programmatic ecosystems, web-based point-and-click platforms have proliferated: the Analyst suite (ExpressAnalyst, MetaboAnalyst, OmicsNet, OmicsAnalyst) [R8], ExpOmics [R41], the single-cell analyst [R6], CFViSA [R40], NOODAI [R33], PhenoMultiOmics [R14] and disease-specific portals such as CPMOAD [R7] and LOSTdb [R34] now offer GUI-driven alternatives that lower the barrier to entry but introduce their own concerns about transparency and reproducibility. Finally, containerised, workflow-management approaches — Nextflow, Snakemake and WorkflowHub-compatible Research Object Crates [R11, R18, R26, R35] — attempt to capture provenance at the level of the analysis environment itself.

Among these application domains, host–microbiome research exemplifies the infrastructural pressure particularly acutely. Microbial community samples bring together metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and metabolomics, with sample coverage that is intrinsically inconsistent across layers because taxa differ in their genomic recoverability, expression detectability and chemical extractability [R1, R54]. As the microbial multi-omics perspective of Van Den Bossche and colleagues emphasises, the complexity of analysing a single isolate is multiplied further when samples comprise hundreds to thousands of individual species, yet standardised workflows and benchmarked datasets remain scarce [R54]. This combination — heterogeneous data formats, inconsistent sample coverage, complex analytical chains and weak reproducibility standards — is precisely what motivated the development of workflow-level solutions such as EasyMultiProfiler (EMP), an R workflow built on SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment that organises extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation into a single coherent pipeline [R1]. Microbiome multi-omics is therefore not just another application area; it is a canonical stress test for any claim that multi-omics software has matured as an infrastructure.

A candid assessment must temper the cataloguing instinct. The sheer number of tools is often taken as evidence of progress, yet the evidence reviewed here describes a field in which each new publication tends to add another integration method rather than consolidate best practice. Benchmarking studies of cancer subtype clustering [R4], multi-omics biomarker discovery [R50] and single-cell integration [R10, R37] consistently find that no single method dominates across datasets, and that gains over simpler baselines are often modest. The persistence of batch effects, platform-specific artefacts and the absence of agreed-upon reference datasets mean that methodological choice — not biological signal — frequently determines the headline result. Tool catalogues lengthen faster than standards mature, and the fragmentation that integration was meant to solve remains, in many respects, intact. The review that follows takes this tension as its starting point: it surveys the available software landscape across general-purpose frameworks, microbiome-centred tools, GUI platforms and containerised infrastructure, examines the limited but informative benchmarking evidence, and uses EasyMultiProfiler as a worked example of what a domain-specific, workflow-level solution can — and cannot — deliver relative to its alternatives.

A useful organising principle for the heterogeneous landscape of multi-omics integration software is the point in the analytical pipeline at which information from different omics layers is allowed to interact. Three regimes are routinely distinguished in the methodological literature: early integration, in which raw or preprocessed features from each omics layer are concatenated into a single matrix and fed to one downstream learner; intermediate integration, in which each omics is first summarised in its own representation and the resulting views are then fused in a joint latent space, graph, or factor decomposition; and late integration, in which omics-specific models are trained independently and their outputs are combined only at the decision or prediction stage. This taxonomy, while inevitably simplified, maps cleanly onto the principal algorithmic families represented in the corpus reviewed here, and it provides a frame against which claims of methodological novelty can be assessed.

Early integration remains the most straightforward strategy and the easiest to implement on top of generic machine-learning toolkits. In its classical form it underlies pipelines that learn patient embeddings or disease classifiers directly from concatenated feature vectors. The MOADLN framework, for instance, uses three fully connected layers per omics and a self-attention module to reduce dimensionality before concatenating the views for downstream classification [R17]. The contrastive adversarial encoder CAEncoder similarly treats the integrated matrix as input to a Vision Transformer trained end-to-end against a CycleGAN-based adversarial objective [R30]. Conceptual schemes such as STATegra formalise early integration through a non-parametric data-combination step that follows a per-omics machine-learning component analysis [R24]. The appeal of this regime lies in its simplicity and in its compatibility with any supervised learner; its principal weaknesses, by contrast, are the curse of dimensionality when omics blocks differ in scale and the implicit assumption that cross-omics interactions can be captured by a single monolithic model.

Intermediate integration has become the dominant paradigm in bulk and single-cell multi-omics research. The most influential instances are joint matrix-factorisation methods and similarity-based fusion algorithms. The MOFA family and its transfer-learning extension MOTL exemplify the factor-analytic branch, projecting each omics into a shared low-dimensional space whose factors can be annotated biologically and used for downstream clustering or regression [R32]. Similarity network fusion and its descendants constitute a parallel branch that constructs per-omics patient graphs and iteratively fuses them into a single affinity matrix; in the recent benchmarking of eight representative early, intermediate and late integration methods on TCGA colorectal cancer data, SNF emerged as the strongest performer on both simulated and real-world datasets [R4]. A more recent wave of intermediate methods adds deep representation learning to this template. DeepMoIC uses autoencoders to obtain compact per-omics embeddings and then incorporates a patient similarity network through a graph-convolutional architecture [R12]; MCluster-VAEs employs a unified variational autoencoder with an attention mechanism to learn cluster-friendly representations in an end-to-end fashion [R22]; MoAGL-SA generates patient graphs from each omics with graph learning and uses self-attention to weight per-omics graph embeddings adaptively before classification [R39]; MO-GCAN combines per-omics graph convolutional networks with a sample-fusion graph attention network for supervised subtyping across eight cancer types [R29]; and TMODINET adds a Dirichlet-based uncertainty estimation head to a self-attention and graph-convolutional backbone to address the trustworthiness of predictions in clinical settings [R9]. The supervised feature-selection framework DIABLO from the mixOmics package sits at the boundary of intermediate and supervised integration, since it constructs sparse latent components that are jointly predictive of phenotypic groups while remaining interpretable as correlated biomarker signatures [R27].

Late integration, in which each omics produces its own prediction that is then aggregated, is conceptually the most modular and the least prone to dominance by the highest-variance view. Software-side support for late fusion is less conspicuous than for the other two regimes, but it is implicitly used whenever pipelines train separate per-omics classifiers or survival models and combine them at the score level, as in parts of the multi-omics biomarker benchmark that compared 20 statistical, machine-learning and deep-learning methods across five cancer datasets [R50]. The reduced representation of each omics to a prediction score also makes late integration attractive when cohorts are partially overlapping and omics blocks differ in availability.

A second axis that cuts orthogonally across this pipeline taxonomy is the degree of supervision. Unsupervised methods dominate the discovery-oriented literature, where the goal is subtype identification, dimensionality reduction or biomarker prioritisation without external labels; representative tools include SNF [R4], MOFA and MOTL [R32], MCluster-VAEs [R22] and the CancerSubtypes package that wraps four unsupervised subtype-discovery approaches with standardised preprocessing [R49]. Supervised methods, in turn, are preferred when gold-standard endpoints such as cancer subtype, drug response or survival are available; DIABLO [R27], MOADLN [R17], MO-GCAN [R29], TMODINET [R9] and the survival-prediction benchmark that evaluated 11 methods across 18 TCGA datasets [R46] all belong to this category. The systematic survival benchmark is notable because it reported that only one of the multi-omics methods, block forest, outperformed a clinical Cox model, providing one of the few head-to-head empirical demonstrations that more elaborate integration architectures do not always yield better predictions than simpler baselines [R46].

Single-cell multimodal integration adds a third dimension to this scheme because it must reconcile modalities measured on the same cell, on matched cells across modalities, or on different cells within a population. The benchmark of 14 protein-abundance prediction algorithms and 18 single-cell integration algorithms on 47 datasets found totalVI and scArches to be the top protein predictors and Seurat, MOJITOO and scAI to be the strongest vertical integrators [R10], while a parallel benchmark of 12 multi-omics integration methods on RNA and ATAC data emphasised that no single method dominates across the six evaluation aspects considered [R37]. Domain-specific tools such as scMGAT for joint RNA, protein, methylation and ATAC integration [R51] and ScSmOP for single-molecule multiomics [R19] further populate this niche.

A critical reading of the literature reveals two persistent limitations of the proposed taxonomy. First, the same architectural template, most prominently the combination of graph attention networks with per-omics encoders, is re-instantiated with minor variations across cancers, omics combinations and prediction tasks [R12, R29, R39, R42, R51], and the accompanying papers typically demonstrate improvement over a small, often self-curated, baseline set rather than over state-of-the-art supervised or factor-analytic methods evaluated under matched conditions. Second, claims about the superiority of early, intermediate or late fusion are rarely supported by rigorous head-to-head evaluation: the CRC benchmark [R4], the survival benchmark [R46], the single-cell integration benchmarks [R10, R37] and the multi-omics biomarker benchmark [R50] all show that the relative ranking of integration strategies is dataset-dependent, and that simpler early or late approaches can be competitive with, or superior to, more elaborate intermediate models in specific settings. The taxonomy is therefore best used as a descriptive device rather than as evidence for any universal methodological hierarchy.

Microbiome research has long grappled with the gap between taxonomy-oriented surveys and functional understanding of microbial communities. The shift toward host–microbiome multi-omics—where metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics and host-response layers must be jointly analysed—exposes a sobering reality: most tools remain optimised for human cohorts and 16S-derived taxon profiles rather than for the cross-kingdom, functional, and non-model contexts in which microbiomes actually live. Aligning heterogeneous meta-omics layers with host molecular phenotypes is therefore the central unmet challenge that distinguishes microbiome-centred integration from generic cancer or single-cell pipelines, and the tools that do exist are unevenly distributed across the problems they claim to solve.

EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) is positioned explicitly as a microbiome-centric workflow that adopts the SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment data structures from Bioconductor to unify storage and analysis across extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation modules [R1]. Its strength is the disciplined decomposition of a multi-step microbiome pipeline into a coherent R-based workflow that reduces methodological inconsistency between meta-omics datasets and improves reproducibility, which the authors themselves identify as a key bottleneck in the field [R1]. EMP's design is well suited to human and mammalian microbiome projects where established reference databases and curated metadata schemas exist. What the publication does not demonstrate, however, is robust performance on non-model host-associated microbiomes or on studies in which metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic signals dominate and reference annotations are sparse. The framework is therefore best understood as a strong template for standardised human host-microbiome research, not yet as a universal solution for cross-kingdom meta-omics integration.

By contrast, gNOMO was built precisely for the underserved non-model organism case, integrating up to three meta-omics levels—metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics—within a Snakemake-managed pipeline demonstrated on the cockroach Blattella germanica gut microbiome [R26]. Its value lies less in statistical novelty than in acknowledging that the absence of well-annotated reference genomes is the rule rather than the exception for invertebrate, environmental and engineered microbiome studies, and that reproducibility tooling must therefore be paired with database-aware assembly and quantification steps [R26]. Notably, gNOMO does not natively incorporate host transcriptomics or metabolomics; cross-kingdom host-microbe alignment remains a manual step, illustrating how far microbiome multi-omics tooling still lags behind host-centric cancer pipelines that benefit from rich TCGA-style resources [R26].

CFViSA takes a complementary, web-based route, offering 79 analytical tools and integrated microbiome and transcriptome pipelines through a point-and-click Scala/AKKA front end backed by R computations [R40]. This lower barrier to entry is attractive for groups without dedicated bioinformatics capacity, but the platform is primarily a statistical and visualisation suite: it does not orchestrate raw metagenomic read assembly, metatranscriptomic mapping or metaproteomic peptide identification, and so the upstream burden of producing coherent meta-omics matrices falls on the user [R40]. As such, CFViSA complements rather than substitutes for dedicated meta-omics engines.

The conceptual roadmaps proposed in recent reviews highlight precisely where these tools underperform. Perspective work on integrating multi-omics technologies to decipher microbiome functions emphasises standardised workflows, FAIR-compliant data objects, benchmarked datasets and community-driven initiatives as prerequisites for credible functional inference [R54], while translational reviews on inflammatory bowel disease argue that gut-microbiota-centred multi-omics must move beyond taxonomic dysbiosis signatures toward quantitative, longitudinally validated, action-linked biomarkers [R58]. Neither roadmap is yet operationally realised by existing microbiome-centred tools, and the available evidence does not establish whether any of them can recover known host–microbe mechanisms from integrated meta-omics in a head-to-head, community-accepted benchmark.

In sum, the microbiome-centred segment of the integration landscape is characterised by uneven coverage: EMP offers a reproducible backbone for human host-microbiome studies [R1], gNOMO pioneers non-model meta-omics reproducibility [R26], and CFViSA democratises downstream statistics [R40], but the field still over-relies on 16S-derived taxonomy, lacks a unified engine for functional meta-omics across kingdoms, and has no consensus benchmark for evaluating these workflows. The most consequential limitation across the board is that none of these tools has been independently demonstrated to outperform alternatives on a shared, functionally annotated meta-omics testbed, leaving their relative accuracy largely an open question.
